title: The Bodyline Series
text:
By 1932 the Australian batsman Don Bradman was scoring runs at a rate never seen before, and England's cricketers had no answer to him. Before the 1932 to 1933 tour of Australia, England's captain, Douglas Jardine, developed a plan with his fast bowlers, above all Harold Larwood of Nottinghamshire.

The tactic, then called leg theory and soon nicknamed bodyline by the press, was to bowl very fast, short balls that reared up at the batsman's body and head, with most fielders packed close on the leg side to catch any defensive shot. There were no helmets. Batsmen had to choose between being hit and offering catches.

It worked on the field. Bradman's average for the series fell to about 57, high for anyone else but around half of his usual level, and England won the series four games to one. But it caused an uproar. In the third Test at Adelaide, the Australian captain Bill Woodfull was struck over the heart and the wicketkeeper Bert Oldfield suffered a fractured skull from a Larwood ball. When the England manager Pelham Warner visited the dressing room, Woodfull was reported as saying that there were two teams out there, one trying to play cricket and the other not. The Australian Board of Control cabled London calling the bowling unsportsmanlike, and the dispute reached political leaders of both countries.

The laws of cricket were later changed to limit such bowling. Larwood never played for England again after the tour.
lesson: A tactic that wins within the rules but breaks the spirit of the game can cost more than the victory is worth. Consider how others will see your methods, not just whether they work.
people: Douglas Jardine, Harold Larwood, Don Bradman, Bill Woodfull
source: Contemporary press reports; Wisden Cricketers' Almanack; David Frith, Bodyline Autopsy (2002)
